blocks.content: This topic goes deeper into the "act" step of the control loop, covering exactly what makes a reconciliation function correct: idempotence, and an honest acceptance that the system is eventually, not instantly, consistent.
1. Reconciliation Is the Act Step, in Depth
blocks.text: 1. Reconciliation Is the Act Step, in Depth

blocks.content: Where the previous topic covered the overall watch-compare-act shape, reconciliation specifically refers to the "act" part, actually doing whatever work closes the gap between current and desired state.

blocks.alt: The specific step where actual, corrective work happens

blocks.content: This is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have, a reconciliation function has to produce the same correct result whether it runs once or is accidentally triggered five times in a row for the same state, exactly the same idempotence property covered for kubectl apply in the kubectl module.

blocks.alt: The same idempotence property already covered for kubectl apply, now at the controller level

blocks.content: 3. The Actual Shape of a Reconcile Function
blocks.text: 3. The Actual Shape of a Reconcile Function

blocks.content: A real reconciliation function follows a consistent shape: fetch the current state, compute the difference against the desired state, and take only the minimal action actually needed to close that specific gap, not a wholesale rebuild every single time.

blocks.alt: Fetch, diff, and take only the minimal action actually needed

blocks.content: This is an important, honest distinction, Kubernetes does not guarantee your cluster reflects a change the instant you make it, it guarantees the cluster will eventually converge to match, usually within moments, but genuinely not instantaneous.

blocks.alt: A real, honest guarantee, eventual convergence, not instantaneous consistency

blocks.content: This is a direct, practical consequence of the level-triggered design covered in the previous topic, if a reconciliation attempt fails partway through, transiently, nothing special has to happen, the loop simply runs again on its next pass and picks up wherever the actual gap still exists.

blocks.alt: A transient failure simply gets retried on the next pass, no special error handling needed

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Reconciliation, the act step of the control loop, must be idempotent, following a consistent shape: fetch current state, diff, take the minimal necessary action.
Kubernetes guarantees eventual, not instant, consistency, and this same design is exactly why a transient reconciliation failure needs no special handling, just a retry on the next pass.
